aliases.name: Martichora
aliases.meaning: transliteration of the Old Persian name

description.summary: A man-eating creature of Persian origin, first described in Greek by the physician-historian Ctesias in the 5th century BCE. The manticore has the body of a lion, the face of a man with three rows of teeth, and a tail tipped with venomous spines or a scorpion's sting.
description.full: The manticore is a legendary man-eating creature of Persian origin, first transmitted into Greek literature by Ctesias of Cnidus, a physician at the Achaemenid Persian court in the late 5th century BCE. In his Indica (preserved in summaries by Photius and quotations in Aelian's De Natura Animalium), Ctesias describes the martichora as a creature of India the size of the largest lion, cinnabar-red in colour, with a human face, blue eyes, three rows of teeth, and a tail like that of a scorpion that could fire venomous spines fore, aft, or sideways. The name is a Greek transliteration of an Old Persian compound 'martyaxwar' / 'martīya-xvāra', meaning 'man-eater'. Aristotle cites Ctesias on the creature in the Historia Animalium, and Pliny the Elder includes it in the Natural History; through these sources the manticore became a fixture of medieval European bestiaries and, by the late 15th century, of English heraldry. The classical descriptions are widely thought to derive from second-hand accounts of the Indian or Caspian tiger, possibly mixed with reports of porcupines or other animals.

etymology.origin: Old Persian compound 'martyaxwar' / 'martīya-xvāra', from martīya ('man') + xvar- ('to eat'). Transliterated into Greek as μαρτιχόρας (martichōras) by Ctesias and corrupted in later manuscripts to mantichōras, the form that gave rise to Latin mantichora and modern English 'manticore'.
etymology.first_use: Late 5th century BCE in the Greek of Ctesias's Indica.

related_phenomena.name: Sphinx
related_phenomena.description: Greek and Egyptian human-faced lion composite

related_phenomena.name: Lamassu
related_phenomena.description: Mesopotamian human-headed winged bull or lion

related_phenomena.name: Leucrocota
related_phenomena.description: Another Indian/African composite reported by Ctesias and Pliny

features.description: The size and body of the largest lion
A human face, with blue eyes in some accounts
Three rows of teeth on each jaw, said to interlock like a comb
Tail tipped with a sting like a scorpion's, with venomous spines that the creature is said to be able to fire forward, sideways, or backward
A voice compared to a trumpet or pipe blended with a trumpet

physical.morphology: A composite quadruped: lion's body, human face, scorpion-like tail. Medieval bestiaries often gave it a Phrygian cap, a heavy mane, and porcupine-like spines.

abilities.ability: Firing venomous spines from its tail
abilities.description: Said to launch poisonous tail-spines with the force of an arrow over considerable distance
Said to devour humans entirely, leaving no trace

habitat_preference: forests and remote regions of India (in Ctesias)
behavior.diet: Human flesh; the name itself means 'man-eater'

range.description: Originally placed in 'India' by Ctesias and his Greek and Latin successors. In medieval bestiaries and heraldry the creature is generic to far-eastern and exotic landscapes.

first_recorded.source: Ctesias of Cnidus, Indica (preserved in Photius and Aelian)

peak_activity_periods.description: Ctesias (late 5th c. BCE), Aristotle (4th c. BCE), Pliny the Elder (1st c. CE), Aelian (3rd c. CE) treat the manticore as an exotic but real Indian beast.
Manticore enters Latin Christian bestiaries via Solinus and Isidore of Seville, and appears in later medieval and Renaissance heraldry from c. 1470 onward.

origins.cultural_roots: Achaemenid Persian oral tradition, transmitted into Greek via Ctesias's experience as physician at the Persian court.
origins.earliest_accounts: Ctesias of Cnidus, Indica (late 5th century BCE), preserved in Aelian's De Natura Animalium (3rd c. CE) and Photius's Bibliotheca (9th c. CE).
origins.folklore_connections: Likely a literary recasting of the Indian or Caspian tiger, exaggerated in transmission and conflated with other animals (notably the porcupine, whose detachable spines may underlie the 'firing tail-spines' motif).

timeline.event: Ctesias of Cnidus describes the martichora in his Indica
timeline.significance: First Greek account of the manticore
timeline.source: Ctesias, Indica (preserved in Photius, Bibliotheca, and Aelian, De Natura Animalium)

timeline.event: Aristotle, in the Historia Animalium, cites Ctesias's account of the martichora
timeline.significance: Embeds the manticore in the classical natural-history tradition

timeline.event: Pliny the Elder includes the manticore in the Natural History (Naturalis Historia, Book VIII)
timeline.significance: Anchors the creature in Latin natural history

timeline.event: Aelian's De Natura Animalium preserves a fuller version of Ctesias's description
timeline.significance: Major source for later Greek and Latin treatments

timeline.event: Manticore appears in English heraldry, notably as a badge of William, Lord Hastings
timeline.significance: Marks the manticore's adoption into Western heraldic tradition
timeline.source: English heraldic records of the late 15th century

history.modern_era: The manticore has become a stock fantasy creature, recurring in Borges's Book of Imaginary Beings, J. K. Rowling's Harry Potter series, and tabletop games such as Dungeons & Dragons, generally drawing on the Plinian / bestiary description rather than directly on Ctesias.

documentary.name: Ctesias, Indica (late 5th century BCE)
documentary.description: Greek-language description of an Indian man-eating creature, the martichora, by a Greek physician at the Achaemenid Persian court.
documentary.analysis: Treated by ancient and modern scholars alike as a probable garbled account of the Indian or Caspian tiger.
documentary.source: Photius, Bibliotheca cod. 72; Aelian, De Natura Animalium IV.21

scientific.name: Garbled tiger and porcupine
scientific.description: The manticore is best understood as a Greek literary distortion of accounts of the Indian or Caspian tiger, possibly merged with the porcupine (whose seemingly 'shot' quills underlie the venom-spine motif).
proponents: Modern classicists and zoologists, summarised in Wilfred H. Schoff's edition of Ctesias and others
evidence_cited: Tiger's size, colour, and ferocity in northern India
Pattern of distortion characteristic of Ctesias

skeptical.name: Literary chimera
skeptical.description: The manticore is a literary creation built up from a kernel of foreign-animal report, embellished by Greek and Latin writers and stabilised by medieval bestiary tradition.
evidence_cited: Clear textual genealogy from Ctesias through Pliny to medieval bestiaries

stories: Ctesias's Indica account of the man-eating martichora
Aelian's preservation of the same account in De Natura Animalium
Bestiary depictions in Latin Christian manuscripts
folklore.beliefs: In antiquity and the Middle Ages, the manticore was generally accepted as a real exotic animal of distant lands.

literature: Pliny the Elder, Naturalis Historia, Book VIII (c. 77 CE)
Aelian, De Natura Animalium (3rd century CE)

film_tv: Manticore (2005 SyFy / Sci Fi Pictures film)
games: Dungeons & Dragons (manticore as a stock monster)
other: Common heraldic charge in English and continental heraldry from c. 1470 onward

research.ongoing_studies: The manticore is studied within classics, the history of natural history, bestiary studies, and heraldry.
